009.name: Many Jobs at Once
009.hitokoto: Employees became a majority only in 1959. Before that, self-employment was normal.
body: Early-modern farmers widely took up nokan yogyo, trade and craft work in the farming off season, and in a survey of 1829 covering what is now Yashio, Saitama, about 250 of some 1,000 households were in off-season trade or a craft. In 1843 the shogunate had the off-season livelihoods of the eight Kanto provinces written up. Lower samurai too eked out the household with piecework such as papering umbrellas. In some villages four households in ten had trade or craft work alongside farming.

Working for an employer became the majority only after the war. In the Labour Force Survey the share of employees among all persons in employment was 42.4% in 1953, passed 50% for the first time in 1959, and reached 64.9% in 1970, 77.4% in 1990, 87.3% in 2010 and 90.6% in 2025. On the figures, employment as the majority way of working is a new product of the 1960s onward.

The restocking can be placed in January 2018, when the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare drew up the Guidelines on the Promotion of Side Jobs and Second Jobs, struck the clause "shall not engage in the business of another company without permission" from the Model Rules of Employment, and put in a new clause allowing side jobs. It was a revision of model rules, not of a statute, but in the record of Diet proceedings remarks containing the word fukugyo, side job, rose from 9 in 2013 to 66 in 2018 and 97 in 2024.

made.label: Pre-modern Off-season side work
made.fact: Early-modern farmers ran wage work and trade in the farming off season as nokan yogyo, and in a survey of 1829 covering what is now Yashio, Saitama, about 250 of some 1,000 households were in off-season trade or a craft. In 1843 the shogunate had a Register of Names in Off-Season Livelihoods in the Eight Kanto Provinces compiled. Lower samurai eked out the household with piecework such as papering umbrellas and lanterns.

discontinued.label: 1959 Employees pass half
discontinued.fact: In the Labour Force Survey the share of employees among all persons in employment was 42.4% in 1953 and passed half for the first time in 1959 at 51.9%, reaching 64.9% in 1970, 77.4% in 1990, 87.3% in 2010 and 90.6% in 2025.

restocked.label: 2018 Side-job guidelines
restocked.fact: In January 2018 the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare drew up the Guidelines on the Promotion of Side Jobs and Second Jobs, and at the same time struck "shall not engage in the business of another company without permission" from the Model Rules of Employment and put in a new provision that "a worker may engage in the business of another company outside working hours". The guidelines were revised in September 2020 and July 2022.

keyfacts.text: Share of employees among all persons in employment, from the Labour Force Survey (long-term time series table 4): 42.4% in 1953 (16.60 million employees out of 39.13 million in employment), 51.9% in 1959, 64.9% in 1970, 77.4% in 1990, 87.3% in 2010, 90.6% in 2025 (61.85 million out of 68.28 million). The self-employed went from 9.91 million in 1953 to 4.99 million in 2025, family workers from 12.62 million to 1.15 million.

Early-modern nokan yogyo was wage work and trade carried on by farmers between the tasks of farming; in the off-season survey of 1829, about 250 of some 1,000 households in what is now Yashio were in off-season trade or a craft. In 1843 a Register of Names in Off-Season Livelihoods in the Eight Kanto Provinces was compiled.

Lower samurai and shogunal retainers eked out the household with piecework such as papering umbrellas and lanterns or teaching in a terakoya school, and the Aoyama Hundred-Man Musketeer Corps produced and sold "Aoyama umbrellas" as an organised business.

In January 2018 the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare drew up the Guidelines on the Promotion of Side Jobs and Second Jobs, deleted "shall not engage in the business of another company without permission" from the duties of compliance in the Model Rules of Employment, and put in a new provision on side and second jobs. The guidelines were revised in September 2020 and July 2022.
In the searchable record of Diet proceedings, remarks containing the word fukugyo, side job, rise from 5 in 2010 to 9 in 2013, 30 in 2016, 66 in 2018, 72 in 2021 and 97 in 2024.

curve.title: Employees as a share of ◆all persons in employment
curve.subtitle: Employees = persons in employment other than the self-employed and family workers

010.name: Mottainai
010.hitokoto: Mottainai went out to the world in 2005, in a Kenyan activist's UN speech.
body: Mottainai is used in A Collection of Tales from Uji (c.1221), of the Kamakura period, and mottainashi is listed in the dictionary Gagakushu of 1444. It first meant improper, or too good for one: "mottainaki aruji kana" in Tales from Uji meant "what an improper master". The present use, regretting that a thing is wasted, is already there in The Chronicle of Great Peace in the second half of the 14th century.

The date this word became a world commodity is 4 March 2005. Wangari Maathai, the Kenyan environmental activist who came to Japan that February, learned mottainai from an interview with the Mainichi Shimbun and proposed in a speech at UN headquarters, "let us spread MOTTAINAI to the world". The same day the Mainichi Shimbun set up a secretariat and the campaign began.

The second restocking took the form of a statute. The Act on Promotion of Food Loss and Waste Reduction, promulgated on 31 May 2019 and in force from 1 October, places a duty to reduce food loss on the state, local governments and businesses. A word that in medieval times also meant improper survived as a word for regret at waste, and came back as the MOTTAINAI slogan and as a statute that calls for an awareness of not wasting food.

made.label: c.1221 Tales from Uji
made.fact: Mottainashi is used in A Collection of Tales from Uji (c.1221), of the Kamakura period, and the dictionary Gagakushu, completed in 1444, has entries for mottai and mottainashi in its section on words. Old-language dictionaries give the senses in the order (1) outrageous, improper (Tales from Uji), (2) too good for one, gratifying (the kyogen play Buaku), (3) a shame, a waste, and today almost only the third is used. No primary source was found, within what this catalogue examined, to show when the third sense became the main one.

restocked.label: 2005 MOTTAINAI
restocked.fact: In February 2005 Wangari Maathai (Nobel Peace Prize, 2004), invited to Japan by the Mainichi Shimbun for events marking the entry into force of the Kyoto Protocol, learned the word mottainai, and on 4 March that year proposed at UN headquarters in New York, at the Commission on the Status of Women, "let us spread MOTTAINAI to the world". The same day the Mainichi Shimbun placed a secretariat within the paper and began the MOTTAINAI campaign. The second restocking is the Act on Promotion of Food Loss and Waste Reduction (Act No. 19 of 2019, promulgated 31 May 2019, in force 1 October).

keyfacts.text: The Muromachi-period dictionary Gagakushu (1444) glosses mottai in its section on words as shotainashi, without proper form, and explains mottainashi as "greatly losing right reason". The Nihon kokugo daijiten gives the first use of mottainashi as A Collection of Tales from Uji (c.1221).

The old-language dictionary gives the senses as (1) outrageous, improper (Tales from Uji 1.15, "ahare, mottainaki aruji kana"), (2) too good for one, gratifying (the kyogen play Buaku, "ah, mottainai, first let me take this hand and help you up"), (3) mottainai, a shame.

The third edition of Kojien (1983) gives three senses, "(1) unseemly towards gods, buddhas or persons of rank; improper. (2) too good for one; undeserved; gratifying. (3) a shame to spend or use up carelessly", and today almost only the third is used.

Wangari Maathai came to Japan in February 2005 at the invitation of the Mainichi Shimbun and met the word mottainai, and on 4 March 2005, in a speech at UN headquarters in New York, proposed "let us spread MOTTAINAI to the world". The same day the Mainichi Shimbun set up a secretariat and began the campaign. She carried it further at Live 8 that July.
The Act on Promotion of Food Loss and Waste Reduction is Act No. 19 of 2019, promulgated on 31 May 2019 and in force from 1 October 2019.
Neither mottainai nor MOTTAINAI is among the words awarded, as grand prize or top ten, in the 22nd New Words and Buzzwords Award of 2005.

011.name: Romantic Love
011.hitokoto: The first use of renai in Japanese is not a book on love but a translation of Self-Help.
body: Renai is not a rewording of the Edo period's iro or koi. The first use cited by the Nihon kokugo daijiten, selected edition, is the phrase "fell deeply in renai" in Saigoku risshihen (1870-71), Masanao Nakamura's translation of Smiles's Self-Help; the word entered Japan tucked inside a textbook of getting on in the world, not a book that talks about love. As a Chinese compound it was already in Lobscheid's English and Chinese Dictionary (1866-69) as a rendering of to love.

In the first years of Meiji it was used as a rendering of love alongside airen and renbo, and renai came to predominate in the Meiji 20s (1887-96). In 1891 Yoshiharu Iwamoto's Jogaku zasshi answered Soho Tokutomi's argument against renai and defended the word, and in February 1892 Tokoku Kitamura wrote "The Pessimist Poet and Womanhood" in the same magazine and declared that "renai is the secret key to human life". Here the word became a norm.

Honyakugo seiritsu jijo by Akira Yanabu (Iwanami Shinsho, 1982) shows that in letters of 1887 Tokoku wrote "love" in katakana and distinguished it from carnal desire, and argues that because the translated word renai was purified into a Western notion that separates soul from body, its realisation became hard to find within Japanese reality. The word arrived in 1870 and became a commodity in 1892.

made.label: 1870 Saigoku risshihen
made.fact: The first use of renai cited by the Nihon kokugo daijiten, selected edition, is in Masanao Nakamura's translation Saigoku risshihen (1870-71): "he once saw a girl of the village, fell deeply in renai, and went to her house". Its note on the word says that from the first years of Meiji it was used alongside airen and renbo as a rendering of the English love, and that renai came to predominate from the Meiji 20s (1887-96). It was made a norm by Yoshiharu Iwamoto in Jogaku zasshi in 1890 and by Tokoku Kitamura's "The Pessimist Poet and Womanhood" in the same magazine in February 1892.

keyfacts.text: The first use of renai in the Nihon kokugo daijiten, selected edition, is in Masanao Nakamura's translation Saigoku risshihen (1870-71): "he once saw a girl of the village, fell deeply in renai, and went to her house".

The same dictionary's note on the word: in China it already appears in Lobscheid's English and Chinese Dictionary (1866-69). In Japan it was used from the first years of Meiji alongside airen and renbo as a rendering of love, and renai came to predominate from the Meiji 20s (1887-96).

The chapter on renai in Honyakugo seiritsu jijo by Akira Yanabu (Iwanami Shinsho, 1982): in letters of 18 August and 4 September 1887, Tokoku Kitamura wrote "love" in katakana and distinguished "the Japanese way of love" from carnal desire. It argues that the translated word renai was purified into a notion separating soul from body, apart from the earlier koi and ai, and that its realisation therefore became hard to find within Japanese reality.

In 1891 Yoshiharu Iwamoto's Jogaku zasshi answered Soho Tokutomi's argument against renai and defended the word, and in February 1892 Tokoku Kitamura published "The Pessimist Poet and Womanhood" in the same magazine, declaring at its opening that "renai is the secret key to human life".

Karyu shunwa (1878-79), Jun'ichiro Oda's translation of Bulwer-Lytton's Ernest Maltravers (1837), depicted love and marriage as an early Meiji translated novel and helped the notion of romantic love take hold.

012.name: Punctuality
012.hitokoto: A foreign instructor in the 1850s wrote that Japanese leisureliness was astounding.
body: On 14 October 1872 (12 September Meiji 5) a railway opened between Shinbashi and Yokohama. The timetable was written in hours and minutes, but what people used was the variable-hour system, which divided day and night each into six, and whose smallest unit, the kohanko, was about 30 minutes. Trains to the minute had begun to run over a reckoning of time whose hours changed length with the season.

Two months later, on 9 November Meiji 5, Grand Council Proclamation No. 337, "The Rescript on the Calendar Change and the Promulgation of the Solar Calendar", was issued; 3 December Meiji 5 became 1 January Meiji 6, and the day switched to fixed hours, 24 to the day. Willem van Kattendijke, the Dutch officer who taught at the Nagasaki Naval Training Centre in the last years of the shogunate, left the words "the leisureliness of the Japanese is astounding". A people that keeps time does not yet exist at this point.

Chikoku no tanjo, edited by Takehiko Hashimoto and Shigehisa Kuriyama (Sangensha, 2001), follows the process by which railways, factories and schools drilled in time discipline, and argues that there was a stretch of the Meiji period when late arrivals on the railways were normal, and that running to time became strict only from about 1900. In 1887 service regulations were made to bring station clocks and conductors' watches into line, and in 1920 the Life Improvement League made 10 June Time Day. Manufacture took half a century.

made.label: 1873 Fixed hours in force
made.fact: On 14 October 1872 (12 September Meiji 5) the railway between Shinbashi and Yokohama opened, with a timetable in hours and minutes. Grand Council Proclamation No. 337 of 9 November Meiji 5, "The Rescript on the Calendar Change and the Promulgation of the Solar Calendar", made 3 December Meiji 5 into 1 January Meiji 6 (1 January 1873), abolished the variable-hour system and switched to fixed hours, 24 to the day.

keyfacts.text: Grand Council Proclamation No. 337 of 9 November Meiji 5, "The Rescript on the Calendar Change and the Promulgation of the Solar Calendar". It made 3 December Meiji 5 into 1 January Meiji 6 and introduced fixed hours, with 365 days to the year and 24 hours to the day.

On 14 October 1872 (12 September Meiji 5) Japan's first railway opened over the 29 km between Shinbashi and Yokohama. From the first day the timetable was in minutes, showing people a finer division of time than the smallest unit of Edo's variable hours, the kohanko of about 30 minutes.
In 1887 the Service Regulations for Staff Employed on Operating Lines were laid down, requiring station clocks and conductors' watches to be brought into line.

Willem van Kattendijke, the Dutch naval officer who taught at the Nagasaki Naval Training Centre in the last years of the shogunate (1857-59), recorded in Nagasaki kaigun denshujo no hibi that "the leisureliness of the Japanese is astounding", giving as examples timber ordered for the tide that did not arrive and workmen who did not come back to the yard.

Chikoku no tanjo: The Formation of Time Consciousness in Modern Japan, edited by Takehiko Hashimoto and Shigehisa Kuriyama (Sangensha, August 2001), follows the formation of time discipline through railways, factories and schools, and argues that there was a stretch of the Meiji period when late arrivals on the railways were normal, and that running to time grew strict only from about 1900.

In 1920, during the "Time" exhibition planned by the Ministry of Education and held at the Tokyo Museum of Education from 16 May to 4 July, the Life Improvement League and other supporting bodies fixed 10 June as Time Day. It derives from the entry in the Nihon shoki on the setting up of a water clock on the 25th day of the fourth month of Tenji 10.

013.name: Maternal Instinct
013.hitokoto: It was a Ministry of Health and Welfare white paper that denied the three-year-old myth.
body: Bosei is held to be a translated word set against the moderskap of the Swedish thinker Ellen Key. By the time Akiko Yosano wrote "Against the Overvaluing of Motherhood" for the February 1916 issue of Taiyo it was current enough to carry a title, and it spread with The Renaissance of Motherhood, translated by Raicho Hiratsuka (Shinchosha, 1919). The first use in the Nihon kokugo daijiten is likewise Takeo Arishima's A Certain Woman of 1919.

In the debate on the protection of motherhood of 1918-19, Yosano, who argued for women's economic independence, was set against Hiratsuka, who held that the state should protect women through pregnancy, birth and child-rearing. The notion that a mother's love is instinct got its word in this period, and in household-education books of the 1910s and 1920s it is stressed as "a heart that gives itself for the child". Before that, as Mikako Sawayama's work shows, child-rearing in early-modern times sat next to borrowed milk and service as a wet nurse, to fostering out, to abandonment and infanticide.

Boseiai shinwa no wana by Masami Ohinata (Nippon Hyoron Sha, 2000) argued that "the maternal" is a myth society produced. A government white paper denies part of it too. The 1998 White Paper on Health and Welfare states plainly that "no rational basis, at least, can be found for the three-year-old myth", and wrote that most of child-rearing can be done by fathers as well. No continuing opinion survey was found, within what this catalogue examined, that tracks approval or disapproval of maternal love itself.

made.label: 1916 The word bosei
made.fact: Bosei is held to be a rendering of the Swedish moderskap of Ellen Key. An early use is Akiko Yosano's "Against the Overvaluing of Motherhood" (Taiyo, February 1916), and it came into circulation with The Renaissance of Motherhood, translated by Raicho Hiratsuka (Shinchosha, 1919). The first use given by the Nihon kokugo daijiten, selected edition, is Takeo Arishima's A Certain Woman (1919). It was widely argued over in the debate on the protection of motherhood of 1918-19, and the word settled in during the Showa period (Nihon joseishi jiten).

keyfacts.text: Nihon joseishi jiten (Shinjinbutsu Oraisha, 1994) takes bosei as a rendering of Ellen Key's moderskap and says it was first used in The Renaissance of Motherhood, translated by Raicho Hiratsuka (Shinchosha, 1919); but Akiko Yosano's "Against the Overvaluing of Motherhood" (Taiyo, February 1916) already uses bosei in its title, so the word was in circulation by 1916.

The first use of bosei in the Nihon kokugo daijiten, selected edition, is Takeo Arishima's A Certain Woman (1919), "an unstoppable consciousness of bosei". Britannica International Encyclopaedia describes motherhood as "not something with which women are instinctively equipped, but a cultural and social attribute".

The debate on the protection of motherhood (1918-19): Akiko Yosano held up women's economic independence and criticised state protection of motherhood as "a doctrine of dependence"; Raicho Hiratsuka, following Ellen Key, argued for state protection of women through pregnancy, birth and child-rearing.

The 1998 White Paper on Health and Welfare states plainly that "no rational basis, at least, can be found for the three-year-old myth", and said that most of child-rearing is possible for fathers too, and that excessive closeness between mother and child can have ill effects.

Edo no chichi to kodomo by Mikako Sawayama (Yoshikawa Kobunkan, 2017) treats early-modern borrowed milk and service as a wet nurse and the relation of abandoned children to milk, and Shussan to shintai no kinsei (Keiso Shobo, 1998) treats measures against infanticide such as the Sendai domain's infant-rearing scheme. Both show that milk and child-rearing were not shut up in the mother alone.
Boseiai shinwa no wana by Masami Ohinata (Nippon Hyoron Sha, April 2000) argues that "the maternal" is a myth society produced. The same author's Bosei no kenkyu appeared in 1988.

014.name: Nudity Is Shameful
014.hitokoto: A fine for going out naked. The article took effect in Tokyo on 13 November Meiji 5.
body: On 8 November Meiji 5 (8 December 1872) Tokyo Prefecture issued the Ishiki Kaii Regulations, the misdemeanour code, and put them in force from the 13th. Five general articles, 23 ishiki offences, 25 kaii offences. Article 22 made "whoever goes naked or bares the upper body, or exposes the thighs and legs, making an unseemly spectacle", and Article 12 "whoever runs a mixed bath for a living", subject to a fine, with caning or detention where it could not be paid. The Grand Council proclamation of 19 July 1873 turned them into the Local Ishiki Kaii Regulations, in 90 articles, and spread them over the whole country.

Behind this were foreign eyes. Perry's Narrative of the Expedition (1856) drew the mixed bathing of a public bathhouse in Shimoda with an illustration, and judged the common people of Japan lewd for all their high morals. Miki Kawabata argues that rulers who had taken the Western gaze inside regarded the old customs as backward and forbade them. Bans on mixed bathing were not a Meiji invention, though: they had been issued and broken again and again since the Edo period, in Kansei-era Edo, in Kyoto in 1843, in a Tokyo notification of 1869.

What was new was that the bans on nakedness issued in Yokohama in 1868 and Tokyo in 1871 were gathered into regulations with penalties, and those made into national law. The regulations were absorbed into the police offences of the Penal Code of 1880, in force from 1882, and passed on to the Police Offences Punishment Ordinance of 1908 and the Minor Offences Act of 1948. The sense that nakedness is shameful has run 150 years without a break in the text.

made.label: 1872 Misdemeanour regulations
made.fact: Tokyo Prefecture notification of 8 November 1872 (Meiji 5), in force from the 13th of the same month. Article 22 of the ishiki offences, "whoever goes naked or bares the upper body, or exposes the thighs and legs, making an unseemly spectacle", and Article 12, "whoever runs a mixed bath for a living", were made subject to a fine; where it could not be paid, an ishiki offence drew caning and a kaii offence detention. The Grand Council proclamation of 19 July 1873 rolled them out nationwide as the Local Ishiki Kaii Regulations, in 90 articles.

keyfacts.text: The Tokyo Ishiki Kaii Regulations were made by a Tokyo Prefecture notification of 8 November 1872 (Meiji 5) and came into force on the 13th of the same month (5 general articles, 23 ishiki offences, 25 kaii offences). The Grand Council proclamation of 19 July 1873 turned them into the Local Ishiki Kaii Regulations, in 90 articles (37 ishiki, 48 kaii), which each locality could add to or cut with the permission of the Police Bureau.

Among the ishiki offences were "Article 12, whoever runs a mixed bath for a living" and "Article 22, whoever goes naked or bares the upper body, or exposes the thighs and legs, making an unseemly spectacle". The Yomiuri Shimbun of 22 January 1876 carries a report of a bathhouse in Hakozaki-cho caught with mixed bathing.

Banning mixed bathing was not a Meiji invention. Mixed baths were forbidden in Edo in the Kansei era (about 1791), in Kyoto in June 1843, at the opening of Tsukiji in 1868, in a Tokyo notification of 1869, and again in Kyoto Prefecture Notification No. 160 of 1871.

Perry's Narrative of the Expedition (1856) drew the mixed bathing of a public bathhouse in Shimoda with an illustration, and judged the lower orders of Japan lewd for all their high morals. The illustration was cut from the later printing.

Miki Kawabata, citing Sumio Ohinata (1992), traces how the accounts of Westerners such as Harris, Perry and Suenson made mixed bathing and nakedness a problem, and how the Japanese side took that gaze inside, regarded the old ways as backward and forbade them.

The Ishiki Kaii Regulations were absorbed into Book 4, "Police Offences", of the Penal Code of 1880 (promulgated 17 July 1880, in force 1 January 1882), and passed on to the Police Offences Punishment Ordinance of 1908 and, after the war, to the Minor Offences Act (1948, exposure of the body).

015.name: Chastity
015.hitokoto: The article punishing a married woman's adultery lost its effect on 15 November 1947.
body: Article 353 of the Penal Code promulgated on 17 July 1880 (Grand Council Proclamation No. 36) punished a married woman's adultery, and the man with her, with major imprisonment of not less than six months and not more than two years. A husband's affair was no crime unless the other party was another man's wife. In February 1899 came the Girls' High School Order (Imperial Ordinance No. 31), and in July that year Education Minister Sukenori Kabayama told the conference of regional school inspectors that the aim of girls' education "lies in laying the groundwork for making them wise mothers and good wives". Chastity was held up by the law and the school alike.

The crime of adultery passed into Article 183 of the Penal Code of 1907 and was deleted by Act No. 124 of 26 October 1947. Yet in January of that same 1947 the Director-General of the Social Education Bureau of the Ministry of Education circulated "On the Implementation of Purity Education", set up a purity education committee the next year, and in 1949 drew up the Basic Outline of Purity Education. The change of name to "sex education" comes around 1970: the norm the law let go of was carried on for a quarter-century by the postwar Ministry of Education.

According to the National Fertility Survey of the National Institute of Population and Social Security Research, the share of unmarried women aged 18 to 34 with no experience of sex fell from 65.3% in 1987 to 36.3% in 2005, then turned back up to 49.4% in 2021, with men back to 44.2%. Chastity as a norm is discontinued, but on the ground the share with no experience of sex is rising again for other reasons. How village customs of premarital relations such as yobai, night visiting, disappeared in modern times is described in works such as Keisuke Akamatsu's Yobai no minzokugaku.

made.label: 1899 Girls' High School Order
made.fact: Article 353 of Grand Council Proclamation No. 36 of 17 July 1880, the Penal Code, punished adultery by a married woman and the man with her with major imprisonment of not less than six months and not more than two years (in force 1 January 1882). Imperial Ordinance No. 31 of 7 February 1899, the Girls' High School Order (published in the Official Gazette on 8 February); at the conference of regional school inspectors in July that year Education Minister Sukenori Kabayama said the aim of higher general education for girls "lies in laying the groundwork for making them wise mothers and good wives".

discontinued.label: 1947 Adultery struck out
discontinued.fact: Following equality under the law in Article 14 of the Constitution of Japan (in force 3 May 1947), Act No. 124 of 26 October 1947, the Act Partially Amending the Penal Code, deleted Article 183 of the Penal Code, the crime of adultery.

keyfacts.text: Penal Code of 1880 (Grand Council Proclamation No. 36 of 17 July 1880, in force 1 January 1882), Article 353: adultery by a married woman drew major imprisonment of not less than six months and not more than two years, and so did the man with her. A husband's infidelity was not punished.
It passed into Article 183 of the present Penal Code (Act No. 45 of 24 April 1907, in force 1 October 1908) and was deleted by Act No. 124 of 26 October 1947.

The Girls' High School Order is Imperial Ordinance No. 31, sanctioned on 7 February 1899 (Official Gazette, 8 February). In July 1899 Education Minister Sukenori Kabayama told the conference of regional school inspectors that it "lies in laying the groundwork for making them wise mothers and good wives; therefore it cultivates a graceful and lofty temper and a mild and chaste nature".

Purity education after the war: January 1947, the Social Education Bureau Director-General's circular "On the Implementation of Purity Education"; 1948, the purity education committee; 1949, the Basic Outline of Purity Education; 1955, "How to Conduct Purity Education (a draft)". It is replaced by "sex education" around 1970.

National Fertility Survey (National Institute of Population and Social Security Research): unmarried women aged 18 to 34 with no experience of sex, 65.3% in 1987, 36.3% in 2005, 49.4% in 2021. Unmarried men, 43.1%, 31.9% (2005), 44.2% (2021).

How the modern norm of chastity drove out the village custom of premarital relations, yobai or night visiting, is described in works such as Keisuke Akamatsu's Yobai no minzokugaku (Akashi Shoten, 1994).

curve.title: Unmarried women aged 18 to 34: ◆the share with no experience of sex
curve.note: The figures for women (the 18-34 total in the same table). It bottoms out in 2005 and turns back up.

016.name: Rising in the World
016.hitokoto: Risshin shusse is already in a kabuki play of 1753. What Meiji made was the content.
body: The four characters of risshin shusse are not a Meiji coinage. The first use in the Nihon kokugo daijiten is the kabuki play Osanago no katakiuchi of 1753, and in the Edo period it meant an ethic of life, keeping to one's station and living frugally in order to "come out into the world and make oneself". What Meiji manufactured was not the word but the content, which was replaced by upward movement through learning and effort.

In 1872 (2 August Meiji 5) the Education System Order was issued with Grand Council Proclamation No. 214, and its preamble taught that "learning is the capital for making one's way" and called on every citizen to attend school. Saigoku risshihen (Smiles's Self-Help), translated by Masanao Nakamura and published two years earlier, and Yukichi Fukuzawa's An Encouragement of Learning, published that same year, became bestsellers, and Risshin shusse shugi by Yo Takeuchi (NHK Books, 1997) describes how this desire became the romance of modern Japan.

In a century and a half the goods have faded. In the Global Survey on Employment and Growth Awareness by Persol Research and Consulting (2022, 18 countries and regions), 19.8% of rank-and-file employees in Japan said they wanted to become managers, the lowest of all, against 90.5% in India, which came first. In 2021 oya-gacha, the parent lottery, entered the top ten of the New Words and Buzzwords Award. The notion that drove out being decided by birth is being driven back by being decided by birth.

made.label: 1872 The Education System Order
made.fact: Grand Council Proclamation No. 214 of 2 August Meiji 5, the preamble on the encouragement of learning: "Learning may be called the capital for making one's way." Saigoku risshihen (1870-71), translated by Masanao Nakamura, and Yukichi Fukuzawa's An Encouragement of Learning (1872) became bestsellers, and risshin shusse turned into the sense of upward movement through learning. The phrase itself is used in the kabuki play Osanago no katakiuchi (1753).

keyfacts.text: The first use of risshin shusse in the Nihon kokugo daijiten, selected edition, is the kabuki play Osanago no katakiuchi (1753): "if only you will hand over the certificate, rising in the world is in plain sight". The phrase exists from the middle of the Edo period.

Encyclopedia Nipponica: in the Edo period risshin shusse was an ethic of life, frugal and holding to one's station, of "coming out into the world and making oneself", but after the Meiji Restoration it was tied to upward social movement and later institutionalised through the school and the bureaucracy.

The preamble to the Education System Order, Grand Council Proclamation No. 214 of 2 August Meiji 5, states that "learning may be called the capital for making one's way" and called on every citizen to attend school.

Risshin shusse shugi: Romance and Desire in Modern Japan by Yo Takeuchi was published as NHK Books in November 1997, with an enlarged edition from Sekaishisosha in 2005. It expands the text of the NHK Ningen Daigaku series (January to March 1996), "Risshin shusse and the Japanese".

In the Global Survey on Employment and Growth Awareness by Persol Research and Consulting (surveyed February to March 2022, published November, 18 countries and regions), rank-and-file employees saying they wanted to become managers were 19.8% in Japan, the lowest of all (India first at 90.5%, Vietnam second at 87.8%).
Oya-gacha was chosen for the top ten of the 2021 U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award, and took the grand prize in the Daijisen New Word of the Year 2021.
